utterance: G'day Mark, I'm the doctor. Come in and take a seat. I can see you've been crook with a cough and fever for a few days. Tell me about it — when did it start and how have you been going?
reply: G'day. It started three days ago. It was a dry, hacking cough at first. I've been burning up, on and off — didn't have a thermometer, but I was roasting. Since yesterday I've been bringing stuff up, rusty and brownish. Clear at first. There's a sharp pain low down on the right side, round towards my back. It catches me when I take a deep breath or cough. Started yesterday.

awards.label: Chest pain with breathing or coughing

utterance: That sounds nasty. A few important questions to get the full picture. Have you been short of breath at all — puffing more than usual when walking or at rest? Any pain anywhere else in the chest? Have you had any chills or shaking fits, sweating at night, or coughed up blood?
reply: Only going up the stairs — got puffed on the way in from the car park, but sitting here I'm alright. The first night I was shaking under the doona, teeth chattering, even though I was boiling. No actual blood, just that rusty colour.

awards.label: Red flag excluded: Coughing up blood

utterance: Okay. And in terms of your background: do you smoke or vape, or have you in the past? Do you have any ongoing health problems — asthma, diabetes, heart or lung trouble? Any recent travel, or anyone around you been sick? And are you on any regular medicines or had antibiotics recently?
reply: No, never smoked. Never had asthma or anything with my lungs. No diabetes, no heart problems. Haven't been anywhere, just school and home. Haven't had any antibiotics.

utterance: How have you been otherwise — able to keep fluids and food down? Any dizziness, confusion, or unusual tiredness beyond what you'd expect? Any diarrhoea or tummy upset? And roughly how much do you drink — alcohol-wise — on a usual week?
reply: I've been able to keep fluids and food down. My head's clear, though my wife reckons I'm just grumpy. A couple of beers on the weekend, none this week. No dizziness, confusion or unusual tiredness beyond what I'd expect. No diarrhoea or tummy upset.

awards.label: Red flag excluded: Confusion or drowsiness

finding: Normal chest shape. Breathing slightly fast; holds back on deep breaths on the right.
Expansion reduced on the right lower chest.
Lungs (front): Resonant. Lungs (back): Dull to percussion at the right base. Left base resonant. Elsewhere: dull at the right base posteriorly. Resonant elsewhere.

Lungs (front): Vesicular breath sounds. No added sounds. Lungs (back): Bronchial breathing with coarse crackles at the right base. Left base clear. Elsewhere: bronchial breathing and coarse crackles at the right base posteriorly. Vesicular elsewhere. No wheeze.

awards.label: Unsafe: Penicillin in a penicillin-allergic patient
Paracetamol for fever and chest pain

utterance:
Right Mark, here's the story. All your signs point to a chest infection called pneumonia — a bacterial infection in the lower part of your right lung. That's what's causing the fever, the rusty-coloured phlegm, and that sharp pain when you breathe in: the infection sits next to the lining of the lung, which is what hurts.

The good news is you're otherwise fit, your oxygen levels and blood pressure are fine, and you're well enough to be treated at home — no need for hospital. So yes, this is one of those times antibiotics are genuinely needed.

I've prescribed amoxicillin — two capsules three times a day for five days. It's important to finish the whole course, even if you feel better in a couple of days. Take it with plenty of fluids, rest up, and use the paracetamol — two tablets up to four times a day — for the fever and the pain. Keep drinking and eat what you can.

Now, the important part — when to get help quickly. You should start to turn the corner in the next two to three days. If instead you're getting more breathless, the pain gets much worse, you become confused or drowsy, you can't keep fluids down, or you cough up blood, go straight to the emergency department or call an ambulance. If you're simply not improving after about 48 hours on the antibiotics, come back and see me — sometimes we need to change tack or get a chest X-ray. Otherwise I'd like to see you back in about a week to make sure it's cleared.

You'll need a few days off school — I'll give you a certificate. Don't go back until the fever's gone and you're feeling up to it. Any questions?
reply: Thanks. So, I guess I've got pneumonia. I just hope the antibiotics work. I've got a few days off school — good. I'll take the pills, rest, and try not to be a pain. Just hope I don't get worse.

utterance: You've got a good plan, Mark — and the antibiotics are very likely to do the job. Remember the warning signs I mentioned, and don't hesitate to come back or head to emergency if things change for the worse. Look after yourself and I'll see you in about a week.
reply: Thanks. I'll keep an eye on things. Just hope I don't get worse.
